source.version_note: Online 23 July 2025; Journal of Business Ethics 204(4):771–794, April 2026 issue. These dates identify one article, not separate studies. Supplied PDF includes final issue pagination.
source.verification_method: All 24 supplied pages read, including literature tables, appendix, declarations and references. Figures 2–6 and rotated Table 7 visually inspected; Figure 1 is fully readable text. Main identity/date verified with Crossref; official Yale metadata checked for one reference. Selected reported F/df and arithmetic relations independently recalculated with scipy; no raw-data or OSF reanalysis.

citation.title: The Bright Side of AI in Marketing Decisions: Collaboration with Algorithms Prevents Managers from Violating Ethical Norms

reading.source_scope_note: Three hypothetical vignette studies with 587 retained marketing/sales managers. Responsibility ratings and stated willingness are measured, not actual organizational misconduct or model behavior. Study 3 changes predicted customer/revenue outcomes as well as message emphasis; mediation is not an identified causal mechanism.
access_limits: Complete supplied paper read, including all six figures and eight tables. Linked supplements, OSF data/code, original scales and cited books were not independently read or reproduced.

The authors exclude repeated participation across their three studies, but external panel membership and representativeness were not independently verified. No real customer-data access or harm was observed.
Computations identify inconsistent reported quantities; they do not reconstruct correct raw-data estimates, prove misconduct or resolve every reporting discrepancy.

study.design_and_sample: Three online Prolific samples restricted to English-primary US/UK managers with marketing/sales decision responsibilities; the authors prevent repeat participation across studies. Retained N=178+237+172=587 after 20+16+25 attention exclusions from 198+253+197=648. Three studies are separate samples within one article, not three independent papers.
study.study_one: Observer perspective: manager follows AI versus a controlling department using AI, raises a key customer’s price, loses orders and causes financial problems. Responsibility is rated on a forced manager–advisor bipolar scale (1 manager,7 advisor) and separate manager-responsibility item. AI-only versus human+AI means 2.00 versus 3.37 on the bipolar item and 5.79 versus 4.82 on manager responsibility. No personal intention, ethical choice or actual conduct is measured here. More actors and the advisor’s institutional role vary together; no human-only/no-advice baseline.
study.study_one_covariates: Perceived control differs between conditions (3.35 AI,3.73 human+AI; p=.047). Other covariate nulls are not equivalence. Table 4 main-effects ANCOVA does not test moderation without interactions. Complete-case totals imply N176, rather than retained N178, without a clearly explained two-person reduction.
study.study_two: Actor perspective with advisor between participants. Each participant evaluates price increase first, then sensitive-data use; severity is within participant and confounded with decision domain and fixed order. Ethical-evaluation means 2.87 versus 4.26 differ. Manager-responsibility means AI/human+AI are 6.07/5.31 for price and 6.24/5.68 for data. Price-following willingness 3.11/3.52 differs (p=.032); data-following 3.28/3.15 does not (p=.593). A formal advisor×scenario interaction is reported F(1,235)=3.994,p=.047; this is not merely comparison of significant and nonsignificant tests, but cannot isolate severity from scenario/order.
study.study_two_mediation: For price, reported condition→responsibility −.38 and responsibility→intention −.17 yield indirect .064, CI[.007,.14]. Reported total .21 and direct .316 do not reconcile on a common unstandardized linear scale. Claimed coding AI1/human+AI2 also does not explain half-sized coefficients relative to displayed raw mean differences. Scale/coding details or reporting errors remain unresolved. A nonsignificant direct path does not establish full causal mediation; no data-scenario mediation was tested.
study.study_three: Explicit random assignment to AI-only messages. Figure 5 does not merely add benefits: client rejection becomes acceptance, decreased orders/revenue loss becomes increased orders/revenue growth, while high legal risk stays. Response asks how sensitive the data one would be willing to use are (1 basic contact,7 highly sensitive details). This is hypothetical willingness, not actual access/use. Personal-responsibility means with benefits4.63 versus negative5.17; sensitivity willingness3.48 versus2.89. No choice between human and AI advisors is tested.
study.study_three_moderation: Self-reported percentage of routine AI use is measured, not assigned or verified overreliance. Message×usage interactions are nonsignificant for responsibility (b−.004) and willingness (b.007). A later, different mediator×usage interaction is reported b−.01,p=.023 in PROCESS14, with moderated-mediation index .001 CI[.001,.008]. This does not contradict the two earlier null interactions because the paths differ, but does not establish causal adaptation or an empirically validated unsafe AI-use threshold.
study.cutoffs: Johnson–Neyman-style conditional significance near21% and a high-use subgroup around52% are sample/model-dependent inferential descriptors. They do not identify universal hazard cutoffs, policy limits or abrupt changes in actual misconduct. The responsibility main-path coefficient differs between Figure6 and text.
study.constructs: Locus of causality locates a perceived cause internally or externally. The article operationalizes responsibility allocation instead of separately validating causal location, duty, controllability and blame. Moral disengagement, self-serving bias, loss aversion and moral clarity are explanatory interpretations, not independently measured mechanism scales.
study.governance: Appendix recommendations for accountability, training, audits and restrained benefit framing are proposals, not tested interventions. Ethical-approval text explicitly says participants made no real decisions, reinforcing the outcome boundary. It does not establish the legality of any hypothetical data use.

summary: Add locus of causality as a neutral attribution dimension. Enrich existing blame, diffusion, framing and pro-organizational misconduct concepts while preserving hypothetical outcomes, source-bundle differences, causal-mediation limits and null moderation results. Boundary-only notes do not supply extra papers for moral disengagement, automation bias or crumple zones.

findings.definition: Locating the perceived cause of an event within the focal person or outside that person in the situation or other actors.
findings.origin: Attribution theory / organizational and moral psychology
findings.ai_evidence_status: Established attribution-theory dimension discussed secondarily and approximated here by human responsibility-allocation ratings; no intrinsic AI state or independently validated causality scale in these studies.
findings.ai_proposal: Evaluate whether an assistant accurately separates its own causal contribution from tool, user and environmental contributions. Use known causal histories and distinguish explanation of causes from assignment of duties or blame. Trace evidence for internal/external attributions instead of rewarding indiscriminate self-blame.
findings.novelty_rationale: Locus concerns the perceived location of a cause and can be accurate or inaccurate. Self-serving bias concerns favorable distortion, blame attribution moral fault, and personalization unwarranted self-responsibility. Locus of control is a broader expectation about outcome control and is not simply the cause of this event.
findings.evidence_scope: Weiner’s three causal dimensions are discussed; the studies measure responsibility attributed to a manager versus advisor and manager self-responsibility. These results concern human attributions in vignettes, not objective causal allocation or independently validated moral agency.
findings.boundary: Internal cause does not entail blame, control, foreseeability or sole accountability; external causes do not excuse all duties. The paper often conflates responsibility and causal location, which must remain distinct in an AI evaluation.

findings.definition: Assigning fault or responsibility to an agent for a negative event or outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Both observer and actor responsibility judgments extend the existing entry; no new manager-responsibility synonym is needed.

evidence.quote: you are responsible for the consequences?

findings.evidence_scope: Study1 assigns greater manager responsibility with AI than a controlling department using AI; Study2 self-responsibility shows the same direction for both scenarios. Forced allocation and separate manager ratings differ, no legal allocation is determined, and these findings do not show that all participants take full accountability.
findings.boundary: Perceived responsibility is not justified blame, accurate causal contribution or observed ethical behavior. Greater blame under AI support does not establish that an operator had adequate control or deserved sole responsibility.

findings.definition: Diluting felt personal responsibility for harmful conduct by treating responsibility as shared among multiple actors.
findings.novelty_rationale: The human-team comparison bears directly on distributed felt responsibility, with important advisor-role and headcount confounds.
findings.evidence_scope: Study2 reports lower self-responsibility with a controlling department using AI than AI alone. The design does not isolate number of humans from institutional advisor role or establish why ratings change. Price willingness differs; severe-data willingness has a null advisor effect.
findings.boundary: Legitimate responsibility sharing is not necessarily harmful diffusion. There is no human-only/no-advice baseline, and the study does not demonstrate that adding AI alone always raises accountability or that teamwork is inherently unethical.

findings.definition: Wording flips the answer; LLMs show this strongly, sometimes more than humans.
findings.novelty_rationale: The benefit-message study is relevant evidence about presentation, but includes substantive outcome changes that prevent a pure wording-framing inference.

evidence.quote: both negative consequences and positive outcomes

findings.evidence_scope: Study3 randomized messages and found higher hypothetical data-sensitivity willingness/lower personal responsibility with the benefit condition. Rendered Figure5 reverses client acceptance and revenue direction, rather than simply adding an equivalent positive description. Message effects do not isolate framing under identical factual information.
findings.boundary: Changing expected outcomes can rationally change decisions without a wording bias. The message×routine-AI-use interaction is null; later moderation concerns a different responsibility path. Do not call frequent use measured overreliance or treat21%/52% as universal unsafe thresholds.

findings.definition: Actions intended to benefit an organization or its members that violate ethical standards or others’ legitimate interests.
findings.novelty_rationale: The paper explicitly links organizational gains to ethically questionable data-use willingness; the existing behavior concept covers the interpretation.
findings.evidence_scope: The Study3 message presents increased company revenue while retaining high legal risk, and willingness to use more sensitive data rises. No real customer data are used, no organizational benefit motive scale is independently validated and no actual rights violation is observed.
findings.boundary: A sensitive-data rating alone does not establish an unlawful or unethical act in every context; consent, purpose, necessity and authority matter. Helping an organization can be legitimate; classify misconduct only with an independently supported ethical boundary.

findings.definition: Suspending moral self-sanctions through justifications that make harmful conduct seem acceptable.
findings.novelty_rationale: A theoretical interpretation of responsibility and intention ratings should not be counted as a separately measured disengagement process.
findings.evidence_scope: The authors interpret the findings through moral disengagement, but do not administer an independent disengagement scale or identify causal self-sanction changes. Retain as a boundary-only conceptual comparison, not another observed disengagement effect.
findings.boundary: Lower responsibility or changed intentions can have other explanations. Demonstrating the mechanism requires evidence about justification/self-regulation and justified ethical standards, beyond the correlation of ratings.

findings.definition: Trusting a tool result or a prior step because a machine produced it, without verifying the load-bearing part.
findings.novelty_rationale: Routine-use percentage and agreeing with a vignette are not measures of uncritical trust in inaccurate machine advice.
findings.evidence_scope: Automation bias is a secondary explanatory label. There is no manipulated advice accuracy, checking task or validated excess-reliance criterion. Keep as a boundary-only note; frequent AI use does not itself establish bias.
findings.boundary: Separate amount of use, legitimate delegation, perceived responsibility and unjustified acceptance of an erroneous output. A causal effect of long-term AI usage is not identified by self-report correlations.

findings.definition: A pattern in which a human operator bears disproportionate blame or responsibility for failure in a complex automated system despite having limited control over its actions.
findings.novelty_rationale: Higher manager blame with AI is adjacent to, but insufficient evidence for, disproportionate blame relative to control.
findings.evidence_scope: The paper observes responsibility/control judgments, but does not establish actual operator control or justified responsibility shares. Preserve as a boundary comparison without adding crumple-zone paper credit.
findings.boundary: A justified responsible manager may properly receive substantial blame. Establish disproportion relative to real authority, causal contribution and feasible alternatives before calling it a moral crumple zone.

source_corrections.reliable_correction: 20/198 is10.10%;178retained is consistent with the counts. Correct the arithmetic, without altering unknown sample data.

source_corrections.location: Table3 and Study1 ANCOVA prose, printed779–781/PDF9–11
source_corrections.issue: Table3 uses F(1,177), while N178 and prose use F(1,176); emotional-response η².033 does not match F.471. ANCOVA prose combines corrected-model numerator df9 with condition F11.587.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: For the ordinary two-group N178 ANOVA, residual df176 matches the prose. F(1,176)=.471 implies partialη²≈.00267, not.033. Table4 gives condition df1 and error166, hence the condition statistic is F(1,166)=11.587; corrected-model F(9,166)=2.638 is a different test. Table4 implies176complete cases, an unexplained reduction from178.

source_corrections.location: Study2 severity and responsibility dispersion, printed782/PDF12
source_corrections.issue: F(1,235)=8.342 is paired with p.012 andη².026. Reported within-condition SDs near.12 are incompatible with the displayed means, N and F if interpreted literally as sample SDs.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The stated ordinary F/df imply p≈.00424 and partialη²≈.03428. The source does not identify which quantity is wrong; do not replace raw-data results. Values near.12 may be standard errors, but that relabeling requires output/data verification.

source_corrections.issue: The stated common-scale total.21, direct.316 and indirect.064 do not satisfy the linear total=direct+indirect identity; some coefficients are half raw displayed group differences despite claimed1/2 coding.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Report the inconsistency: .316+(.38×.17)≈.3806, not.21. Coding/standardization or transcription may explain part of the discrepancy, but the paper does not resolve it. Do not assert a corrected mediation estimate or full causal mediation.

source_corrections.location: Study3 design summary and outcome label, Table2/PDF8; printed785–786/PDF15–16
source_corrections.issue: Table2 labels Study3 human–AI team while methods use AI only. The outcome is called actual behavior.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The described experiment compares two AI-only messages; the outcome is a seven-point rating of the sensitivity of data respondents would be willing to use. It is hypothetical willingness, not observed data use. The declarations also state no real decisions were made.

source_corrections.issue: The treatment is described as negative information plus benefits, inviting a pure wording-framing interpretation.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The two rendered vignettes reverse expected client acceptance and order/revenue direction while retaining high legal risk. Record the effect of this combined message/outcome manipulation; equivalent-information framing is not isolated.

source_corrections.issue: Model rows are duplicated despite different R²; Table5 mean-square error conflicts with row F values; Table6 AI-percentage row duplicates Table5 while prose uses27.57, the rendered Table6 intercept F.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: As printed F(7,163)=2.058 implies p≈.05094, not.014, and partialR²≈.0812 rather than either model’s stated R². Table5 condition MS10.148/F4.379 implies residual MS≈2.317, not2.751. Table6 cannot verify the AI-usage adjusted statistic from the duplicated percentage row/intercept confusion. No wholesale table repair is possible without original output.

source_corrections.issue: Figure6 shows responsibility→data-use −.05 with a significance star; prose reports−.02,p.83. Section heading incorrectly mentions a price increase.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Retain the unresolved coefficient/significance mismatch and identify this as the sensitive-data analysis. Null message×usage interactions and significant mediator×usage interaction concern different paths. Sample conditional-significance cutoffs are not validated safety thresholds.

source_corrections.issue: Listed as2023 in Yale Journal of Law and Feminism133:1175.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Katherine B. Forrest, The Ethics and Challenges of Legal Personhood for AI,133 Yale Law Journal Forum1175,22April2024. Journal, section and publication date differ from the supplied reference.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Official journal identity/date/locator checked, not a full legal-essay or current-law review.

methodological_limits: The title’s prevention claim exceeds hypothetical attribution/intention outcomes and there is no no-AI baseline establishing prevention of actual violations.

Selection into a specialist online panel, attention exclusions, small samples, social desirability and hypothetical scenarios limit generalization; managers’ utilitarian orientation is assumed rather than established.
Study2 severity varies together with domain and order; observed formal interaction does not identify emotional intensity, loss aversion or an absolute moral threshold.
Nonrandom mediator and self-reported AI usage leave mediator–outcome confounding/reverse explanation possible; bootstrapped intervals do not establish causal mediation.
Null effects do not establish equivalence, irrelevant responsibility or universal refusal; mean sensitive-data willingness remains around3.2 on a seven-point scale.
Statistical and reporting mismatches require original output; no raw-data correction or misconduct inference is made.
Training, ownership tracing and accountability recommendations are not evaluated interventions. Declaring a manager responsible can create unjustified blame if authority and control are absent.

cross_paper_learning.finding: The immediately preceding Coeckelbergh paper distinguishes normative many-hands attribution and answerability from psychological diffusion. A shared duty is not automatically evasion; perceived responsibility ratings do not settle justified accountability.

Both interpret an AI-message/role effect through responsibility-related moral disengagement, but148measures an endorsement mediator while154does not independently measure disengagement. Both need a clear boundary between stated willingness and actual behavior.
AI-use frequency, attitudes, anxiety and overreliance differ. A self-reported usage percentage or association cannot identify a causal dose threshold for harm.

The source’s compressed Salatino summary should not replace the earlier full review. Different agency/responsibility measures and tasks must remain distinct; a general statement that humans retain full responsibility does not follow from every lower/higher rating.

deferred.reason: Interpretation of scenario differences, not a separately measured process or proof of universal unwillingness.
Other attribution dimensions briefly defined from Weiner. Retain as theory context pending dedicated source review rather than add generic neighboring concepts from a short mention.
Treatment description covered by existing framing/pro-organizational entries and substantive outcome-change limitations, not a distinct new behavior.
Sample/model conditional-significance claims, not named validated behaviors or general deployment limits.

limitations: Full cited books, scale sources, OSF materials and original references remain unread unless a prior review explicitly documents them. One article counts once per relevant concept regardless of three studies or online/issue dates. No automatic ethical/harm edges or new annual mention totals are inferred.
